Estuarine thryssa (Thryssa aestuaria) is a small, short-lived clupeiform fish inhabiting brackish waters along tropical and subtropical coastlines. Field surveys indicate that the maximum recorded total length for this species is 13.8 centimeters [Li = 13.8 centimeters], a modest size that reflects its position within a lineage of diminutive forage fishes. Populations in the Sundarbans delta have been closely monitored to document life-history benchmarks under natural thermal regimes. At the standard experimental temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], embryogenesis proceeds rapidly, with the yolk-sac larva emerging from the chorion a mere three days [ab = three days] after fertilization, a developmental pace consistent with the warm-water ecology of the species. This brief incubation period minimizes the duration of egg vulnerability to benthic predators and episodic hypoxia, both of which are common stressors in the soft-sediment habitats the species frequents.

Reproductive output in Thryssa aestuaria has been quantified through captive spawning trials and field-based gonad analyses. Females exhibit a maximum daily reproduction rate of roughly 27.5 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 27.5 eggs per day] under optimal conditions sustained at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], a value derived from the product of batch fecundity and spawning frequency. Individual spawning events yield between 25 and 30 eggs per batch, and females may release such batches nearly daily during peak reproductive windows. This fecundity is paired with an exceptionally small egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, from which the wet weight at birth is calculated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value that underscores the extremely altricial state of the newly hatched prolarvae. The minute size of the yolk-sac larva imposes a tight energetic constraint on the interval to first successful exogenous feeding.

Somatic growth in this species follows a predictable allometric trajectory. Using the length-weight relationship established for local populations, the body mass of an individual reaching puberty at a total length of 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters] corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 3.25 grams [Wwp = 3.25 grams]. This milestone marks the onset of vitellogenesis and active gametogenesis, a considerable energetic investment for such a small-bodied teleost. In contrast, an individual that has attained its asymptotic length of 13.8 centimeters [Li = 13.8 centimeters] achieves an ultimate wet weight of 21.56 grams [Wwi = 21.56 grams], representing the upper bound of body size for this species. The nearly sevenfold increase in mass between puberty and asymptotic size reflects a growth pattern that prioritizes early reproductive output while continuing to increase body mass, a strategy typical of many small, iteroparous clupeiforms inhabiting productive estuarine environments.

Lifespan and senescence patterns have been examined through mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age validation. The oldest documented individuals, maintained in controlled laboratory aquaria at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], have a maximum longevity of 350 days [am = 350 days], a relatively brief total lifespan that places the species among the shorter-lived members of the Engraulidae. Given the rapid maturation schedule, this lifespan allows for multiple reproductive seasons, with females capable of initiating gametogenesis well before reaching half their potential maximum age. The elevated metabolic costs imposed by the consistently warm thermal regime likely contribute to the accelerated physiological pace observed, as individuals progress from larval emergence through senescence within a single annual cycle. Field records from the Hugli estuary corroborate this compressed timeline, with few individuals exceeding eleven months in age.

Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the reproductive strategy of Thryssa aestuaria is finely tuned to its variable habitat. The age at birth of three days at 27.5 °C is among the shortest reported for Indo-Pacific thryssas, a trait that may confer an advantage in turbid, predator-dense nursery zones. Similarly, the ultimate total length of 13.8 centimeters [Li = 13.8 centimeters] and the corresponding maximum body mass of 21.56 grams [Wwi = 21.56 grams] align closely with the values reported for Thryssa purava, a morphologically similar species from the same geographic region. The total length at puberty of 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters] represents roughly 54 percent of the asymptotic length, a proportion consistent with the general pattern observed in small estuarine clupeiforms that mature early to capitalize on ephemeral pulses of planktonic productivity before mortality risk escalates later in the season.
